name: Customer Demand Evidence
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Reading the Fine Print: What Counts as Real Demand in Quantum Computing
lesson.summary: Press releases about quantum computing partnerships and customers can mean very different things, from a paid multi-year contract to a free pilot for marketing purposes, so evaluating genuine demand requires looking past headline counts to the structure of the deal.
lesson.body:
Quantum computing companies routinely announce "partnerships" with recognizable brands in banking, aviation, pharmaceuticals, and automotive manufacturing, and these announcements are often presented, implicitly or explicitly, as evidence of market traction. But as the previous chapter's three buyer types make clear, a partnership announcement can describe several very different underlying arrangements, and only some of them constitute genuine customer demand in the ordinary business sense.

At one end of the spectrum sits a recurring, paid production contract: a customer sends money on an ongoing basis because it is using the quantum company's product to do something it needs done. At the other end sits a joint research grant, where the quantum computing company is actually being paid, often by a government program, to do research work that a big-name corporate partner merely co-signs for visibility and access to results. In between sit free or heavily subsidized pilot programs, offered by the quantum company for its own marketing value, and non-binding memoranda of understanding, which commit neither party to spend anything at all. All four of these can be described in a press release using nearly identical language, "X and Y today announced a strategic partnership," which is precisely what makes headline partnership counts an unreliable signal on their own.

Distinguishing between them requires asking a small number of concrete questions. Does money actually change hands, and in which direction, toward the quantum company or away from it? Is the arrangement recurring, with a renewal or expansion that has already happened at least once, or is it a single announced pilot with no disclosed follow-up? Does the customer itself disclose the spend in its own financial filings or investor communications, which would be an independent signal, or does the figure and framing only ever appear in the quantum company's own materials? A relationship that survives all three questions looks much more like real demand than one that fails them.

Applying this lens across the industry since the early 2020s, pharmaceutical and financial-services firms in particular have participated in dozens of publicized pilots involving problems like molecular simulation and portfolio or risk optimization. The honest, if unglamorous, observation is that the number of those engagements that are known to have converted into a recurring, independently disclosed, paid production relationship, rather than remaining a one-time research collaboration, appears to be very small. This is a qualitative pattern rather than a precisely counted statistic, since neither side always discloses enough detail to verify conversion rates rigorously, but the pattern is consistent enough across public reporting to be a fair basis for skepticism.

The reason this evidentiary bar matters is that it separates subsidized exploration, which the earlier chapter showed large organizations can sustain indefinitely at negligible cost, from genuine commercial necessity, which is what a sustainable revenue model ultimately requires. The next chapter applies this bar systematically across the industry and asks what remains once free pilots, grants, and unbound memoranda are set aside.
